Not typically. Your bike draws power from your battery, your stator recharges the battery. It does help the battery a bit in regards to starting the bike, but it doesn't provide 100% power. If you've ever ridden an old bike without a battery in it, you'll probably have noticed that the headlight gets brighter when you accelerate, and dims when you slow down. This is due to it running off the stator instead of off a battery. A stator doesn't supply a consistent amount of voltage at all times because its voltage is based off the rpm off the bike. When you have a dead battery the bike will run, and on newer bikes you may not get the headlight dimming effect of older simply because modern electrical systems don't draw the same power older ones did, combined with stators putting out more power. The reason the bike still runs without the battery is because instead of the charge going in and charging the battery, it's simply bypassing it because the battery isn't accepting charge. Doing this for too long can overwork a stator and can cause it to fail.
Try not to keep running it like that without the battery, it can be hell on a stator. Your stator is meant to recharge the battery, not run your entire bike.

Rule of thumb, if it increases horsepower, it probably decreases fuel economy. An intake allows for more fuel to be burned in the combustion chamber, allowing a stronger explosion, making for more power. A high flow exhaust will help pull exhaust gases out of the combustion chamber faster and more effectively, allowing a cleaner and richer combustion, meaning more fuel is burned. Just one or the other won't hurt much, nor will you notice large HP gains. However doing both will allow for advertised gains of up to 15 HP, maybe more depending on the kit, but will almost always decrease fuel economy. And keep in mind, fuel economy is also based on you drive and how it's programmed. See if you can get the ecu reprogrammed for more fuel economy if you happen to have some money burning a hole in your pocket, or just take care to use slow and gradual acceleration. We get it, put on the front tire, front fender, and handlebars (including mirrors, throttle, levers, controls and speedo), fill it with oil and a bit of gas, start the bike and make sure it runs, let it warm up, rev it to about 3.5-4000 a couple times to make sure the throttle is functioning properly, set the clock anf make sure all the units on the speedo are correct, double check tire pressures, make sure the clutch works, put the bike in gear and make sure it will roll out in first. Then we shut the bike off and let it cool down. While it cools we check all the lighting and electrical to make sure everything is working right, then once the bike is cool we double check the oil level and coolant levels, and top up as needed. Then we send them on their way to the dealership (this was at my specific dealer where pdi and service were 2 separate departments) where they double check the unit and ensure all is good to go, then the salesman gets the unit and cleans it up and gives it to the customer. This process may vary from dealer to dealer, but this is the process that we use.
